queries.hook: The wish to understand what these texts teach, and to find in them something steady to lean on.
queries.diagnose: When life is lived only for what passes, the heart feels empty; meaning is missing when we forget what does not pass.
queries.steady: What passes cannot fill the heart; turning toward what lasts gives each day a quiet purpose.

hook.speaker: Krishna
hook.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on simple, wholehearted devotion.
hook.sanskrit: पत्रं पुष्पं फलं तोयं यो मे भक्त्या प्रयच्छति । तदहं भक्त्युपहृतमश्नामि प्रयतात्मनः ॥
hook.line: A leaf, a flower, a fruit, a little water: whatever is offered with love, I accept.
hook.translation: Whoever offers me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water, that offering of love from the pure-hearted I accept.
hook.why: Small offerings given with love matter; no one is beyond turning around.

alternates.speaker: Krishna
alternates.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the power of understanding to end confusion and guilt.
alternates.sanskrit: तद्विद्धि प्रणिपातेन परिप्रश्नेन सेवया । उपदेक्ष्यन्ति ते ज्ञानं ज्ञानिनस्तत्त्वदर्शिनः ॥
alternates.line: Learn from those who have seen the truth: approach with humility, ask real questions, and serve.
alternates.translation: Learn it by bowing down, by questioning, and by service. Those who are wise and have seen the truth will teach you that knowledge.
alternates.why: Learn humbly, trust the process, and cut through doubt to act.

prasang.title: The glory of knowledge
prasang.summary: Krishna praises knowledge: learn it humbly from those who know, it carries even the worst wrongdoer across, faith and self-control bring it, and doubt destroys. He ends: cut your doubt and stand up.
prasang.lesson: Learn humbly, trust the process, and cut through doubt to act.

alternates.speaker: Krishna
alternates.setting: Krishna to Arjuna, describing the qualities of the person dear to God.
alternates.sanskrit: सन्तुष्टः सततं योगी यतात्मा दृढनिश्चयः । मय्यर्पितमनोबुद्धिर्यो मद्भक्तः स मे प्रियः ॥
alternates.line: Always content, self-disciplined, firm in resolve, heart and mind given to the divine: such a person is dear to me.
alternates.translation: ever content, steady in practice, self-controlled, firm in resolve, with mind and understanding given to me, that devotee of mine is dear to me.
alternates.why: Kindness without hatred, steadiness in praise and blame: that's what's loved.

prasang.summary: Krishna lists the marks of one dear to him: no hatred, friendly and compassionate, forgiving, content, disturbing no one and disturbed by no one, the same in praise and blame.
prasang.lesson: Kindness without hatred, steadiness in praise and blame: that's what's loved.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on simple, wholehearted devotion.
verse.sanskrit: पत्रं पुष्पं फलं तोयं यो मे भक्त्या प्रयच्छति । तदहं भक्त्युपहृतमश्नामि प्रयतात्मनः ॥
verse.line: A leaf, a flower, a fruit, a little water: whatever is offered with love, I accept.
verse.translation: Whoever offers me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water, that offering of love from the pure-hearted I accept.
verse.why: Small offerings given with love matter; no one is beyond turning around.

prasang.title: The glory of selfless devotion
prasang.summary: A leaf, flower, fruit or water offered with love is accepted. Offer everything you do; the divine hates no one, and even a wrongdoer who turns wholeheartedly is counted good.
prasang.lesson: Small offerings given with love matter; no one is beyond turning around.

verse.meaning: Krishna tells Arjuna that devotion does not demand wealth or perfection. A simple leaf, a flower, a fruit, or a little water, when offered with love, is fully received. The divine accepts what is given from a pure heart and hates no one, which means even a wrongdoer can turn around and be counted as good. The point is that the size of the gift does not matter. The love behind it is what is taken in.
verse.for_you: The searching you feel now is the space where small offerings become enough. A grandparent's quiet morning, a grandchild's call, the warmth of a cup of tea. These are the leaves and water you are being asked to offer.
verse.try_today: Notice one small thing you receive today and let it stand as enough.
verse.scene_line: You stand at the kitchen table with a cup of tea, offering your morning to the day.
asks: What is the smallest thing I can offer today?
Can I let go of needing this day to mean something?

verse.speaker: Prajapati's teaching (narrator)
verse.setting: On the self in the heart that we visit nightly in deep sleep without knowing it.
verse.sanskrit: अनृतापिधानास्तद्यथापि हिरण्यनिधिं निहितमक्षेत्रज्ञा उपर्युपरि सञ्चरन्तो न विन्देयुरेवमेवेमाः सर्वाः प्रजा अहरहर्गच्छन्त्य एतं ब्रह्मलोकं न विन्दन्त्यनृतेन हि प्रत्यूढाः ॥
verse.line: Like people walking daily over buried gold, we pass our own treasure every day and never find it.
verse.translation: As people who do not know the spot walk again and again over a hidden treasure of gold buried in the ground and do not find it, so all these creatures go day after day into that world of Brahman and do not find it, for they are carried away by untruth.
verse.meaning: In the Chhandogya Upanishad, a narrator tells us about a hidden treasure buried under the ground. People walk over it every single day without ever knowing it is there. They are looking everywhere else, so they never find what is right beneath their feet. The verse proposes that we are like those people. We pass over the deepest part of ourselves every night in deep sleep, and we do not find it. We are carried away by untruth, which means we do not recognize what is already here.
verse.for_you: You have walked over your own inner life for decades, never knowing it was a treasure. The search for what it is all for is not about finding a new path, but about seeing the ground you are already standing on.
verse.try_today: Notice one ordinary thing today without trying to name its use.
verse.scene_line: You are walking over a buried treasure of the self every morning.
asks: How do I recognize a treasure I do not know is there?
What is the untruth that carries me away?
Is the self I visit in sleep the same one I seek?

verse.speaker: Lakshman
verse.setting: After Sita is taken, Lakshman comforts Ram, who is lost in grief.
verse.sanskrit: आश्वसिही नरश्रेष्ठ प्राणिनः कस्य नापदः। संस्पृशन्त्यग्निवद् राजन् क्षणेन व्यपयान्ति च॥
verse.line: Take heart. Trouble touches everyone; it flares up like fire and passes.
verse.translation: Take heart, best of men. Which living being does trouble not touch? Troubles strike like fire, king, and pass in a moment.
verse.why: In devastating loss, a steady friend can stop grief from turning into destruction.

prasang.title: Ram's grief and Lakshman's counsel
prasang.summary: Ram returns to an empty hut. He searches, questions trees and animals, breaks down and finally rages that he will destroy the world. Lakshman calms him: don't punish the whole world for one person's crime; trouble comes to everyone and passes.
prasang.story_hook: He came back to the hut calling her name, and no one answered.
prasang.lesson: In devastating loss, a steady friend can stop grief from turning into destruction.

verse.meaning: Lakshman speaks to Ram in the Aranya Kanda after Sita has been taken. Ram returns to the empty hut, questions the trees and animals, and finally breaks down in rage, ready to destroy the world for this loss. Lakshman steps in and says to take heart. He asks Ram which living being is untouched by trouble, saying that trouble strikes like fire and passes in a moment. The verse proposes that a steady friend can stop grief from turning into destruction.
verse.for_you: You have carried a long life and now you are looking for a deeper ground to stand on. You are not broken, but you are searching, and that is a hard place to be. You do not need to build a new self.
verse.try_today: Notice one thing that is steady and true in your morning.
verse.scene_line: You stand in the empty hut of your own searching, and the fire of your grief flares up.
asks: How can I find the ground beneath me when I am searching?

verse.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse.setting: From 'Worship of Shiva': gratitude for a simple life.
verse.sanskrit: यदेतत्स्वच्छन्दं विहरणमकार्पण्यमशनं सहार्यैः संवासः श्रुतमुपशमैकव्रतफलम् । मनो मन्दस्पन्दं बहिरपि चिरस्यापि विमृशन् न जाने कस्यैष परिणतिरुदारस्य तपसः ॥
verse.line: Freedom, simple food, good company, learning that brings calm: what did I do to deserve this?
verse.translation: This freedom to wander at will, food eaten without humiliation, living among noble people, learning whose only fruit is calm, a mind that stirs only gently even when it looks outward for long: I do not know what generous austerity this is the fruit of.
verse.why: Gratitude for a simple life, and devotion without rivalry between forms of God.

prasang.title: Vairagyashatakam: Worship of Shiva
prasang.summary: Devotional verses longing for a quiet life by the Ganga in Shiva's presence, including a famous non-sectarian line that Shiva and Vishnu are one in essence.
prasang.lesson: Gratitude for a simple life, and devotion without rivalry between forms of God.

verse.meaning: Bhartrihari speaks to the reader from a place of deep quiet, looking back at a life that has stripped away its noise. They see freedom to move without asking, food eaten without shame, and learning that brings no storm. They ask what quiet sacrifice earned this. The verse holds that a simple life, good company, and a mind that stirs gently are not small things but the result of a generous austerity we do not recognize. It is a confession of gratitude for what remains when the striving stops.
verse.for_you: You are looking at a day that offers no grand answers, only the quiet arrival of a meal without humiliation and the space to breathe. In the middle of your family's worry, this freedom to sit still is the treasure you have been walking over.
verse.try_today: Notice one small thing today that you did not earn.
verse.scene_line: You sit in the quiet of a room that belongs to no one else.
asks: How do I see this calm as a gift, not a loss?
What did I give up that made this possible?
Can I accept this without wanting more?

verse.speaker: Vasishtha
verse.setting: Vasishtha, after Janaka's story, praises clear understanding (prajna).
verse.sanskrit: य एव यत्नः क्रियते बाह्यार्थोपार्जने जनैः । स एव यत्नः कर्तव्यः पूर्वं प्रज्ञाविवर्धने ॥
verse.line: Put the effort you spend earning money into growing wiser first.
verse.translation: The very effort people put into earning outer wealth should first be put into growing wisdom.
verse.why: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.

prasang.title: King Janaka overhears the sages and keeps ruling, with a free mind
prasang.summary: Walking in his spring garden, King Janaka overhears hidden sages singing about the self. Shaken, he climbs to his palace roof and questions everything he has lived for. When his doorkeeper calls him to the day's work, he decides not to run away: he gets up and does his duties, but with a mind that no longer clutches.
prasang.story_hook: One spring morning, a king out for a walk overheard a song that he could not stop thinking about.
prasang.lesson: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.

verse.meaning: Vasishtha speaks to Rama after telling him about King Janaka. Janaka is walking in his spring garden and overhears sages singing about the true self. He is shaken to his core. He climbs to his palace roof and questions everything he has lived for. When his doorkeeper calls him to his duties, he decides not to run away. He gets up and does his work, but with a mind that no longer clutches.
verse.for_you: The effort you once put into earning a living can now go into growing wiser. You do not need to leave your life to find what you are looking for. You can sit with your family and let your mind rest. Let your own company be enough.
verse.try_today: Spend ten minutes with your grandchild without trying to teach or fix anything.
verse.scene_line: You are in your own quiet garden, hearing a truth that changes everything you thought you knew.
asks: How do I grow wiser when my days feel so quiet now?
How do I sit with my family without trying to fix their pain?

verse.speaker: Seer
verse.setting: Follows the call to enjoy by letting go: how to live and work.
verse.sanskrit: कुर्वन्नेवेह कर्माणि जिजीविषेच्छतꣳ समाः । एवं त्वयि नान्यथेतोऽस्ति न कर्म लिप्यते नरे ॥
verse.line: Do your work and wish to live a full hundred years. Done in this spirit, action does not cling.
verse.translation: Doing your work here, you may wish to live a hundred years. For you there is no other way than this: done in this spirit, action does not cling to a person.
verse.why: Hold what you have lightly, keep working, and see yourself in everyone.

prasang.title: The Isha: enjoy by letting go
prasang.summary: Eighteen verses that open by saying everything belongs to the divine, so we should enjoy it without grasping. They go on to say we should work a full life without being bound, and see ourselves in all beings.
prasang.lesson: Hold what you have lightly, keep working, and see yourself in everyone.

verse.meaning: The Seer speaks to the reader about the way to live and work. They say that you could do your work and wish to live a full hundred years. The idea is that action does not cling to you when you do it in this spirit. You keep what you have lightly, you keep working, and you see yourself in everyone.
verse.for_you: You have stepped back from the daily earning, the way the verse says. Now the work is to see the life you have lived in the people around you. Your grandchild carries something of you forward, and your family holds the shape of your years.
verse.try_today: Notice one small act of care you do for your family today.
verse.scene_line: You are living the full hundred years the Seer spoke of.
asks: How do I let my work go without feeling empty?
How do I see myself in my family now?
How do I wish for a full life without grasping?

story.title: The proud ascetic, the housewife and the butcher
story.story_hook: A young yogi glared at a crow and it fell dead, and for the rest of the day he was sure he had become a very great man.
story.summary: A young ascetic who can burn a bird with a glance is humbled by a housewife who knows what he did, and she sends him to a butcher in the market for teaching. The butcher, doing his trade honestly and caring for his parents, teaches him the highest truth. Doing the duty in front of you, without attachment, is itself the path.
story.lesson: No honest work is beneath you; doing it well is the practice.
story.hook_title: A young yogi burned a crow with a glance, and a housewife put him in his place
story.teaser: A young yogi burned a crow with a glance, and a housewife put him in his place
story.for_you: You have spent a life doing things, and now the doing has stopped. This story says the search for a deeper life is not about finding a new grand purpose, but about bringing the same honest care to the small tasks that remain.
asks: How do I find meaning in a life that is no longer full of tasks?
What does it mean to do my work without clinging to it?
Can I learn from the people I see every day?
